problem: Added qualifier 'relative to the population' not in the source, which says only that the relative position of the central federal power is continually displaced.
replacement: The relative position of the central federal power is continually shifting. Forty years ago most of the citizens of the Union lived on the Atlantic coast, in the area around the spot where Washington now stands. But the great body of the people is now moving inland and to the north, so that within twenty years the majority will undoubtedly be on the western side of the Alleghanies. If the Union continues to exist, the basin of the Mississippi is clearly marked out, by its fertility and its size, as the future center of the Federal Government. In thirty or forty years that region will have taken the rank that naturally belongs to it. It is easy to calculate that its population, compared to that of the Atlantic coast, will be, in round numbers, as 40 to 11. In a few years the States that founded the Union will lose the direction of its policy, and the population of the valley of the Mississippi will predominate in the federal assemblies.

problem: (1) 'almost as much to the point as the act itself' is awkward and shifts the sense of 'there is almost as much in the possibility'. (2) The split of the long sentence detaches 'it is easy to perceive' from the claim that the South is becoming more irritated, which is then stated outright (his hedge dropped).
replacement: It is hard to imagine a lasting union between a rich, strong people and a poor, weak one, even if it were proved that the strength and wealth of the one are not the causes of the weakness and poverty of the other. But union is harder still to maintain when one party is losing strength and the other is gaining it. This rapid and disproportionate growth of certain States threatens the independence of the others. New York, with its 2,000,000 inhabitants and its forty representatives, might perhaps succeed in dictating to the other States in Congress. But even if the more powerful States make no attempt to overbear the lesser ones, the danger remains, for the possibility of the act matters almost as much as the act itself. The weak generally distrust the justice and the reason of the strong. The States that grow less rapidly than the others look with envy and suspicion on those that fortune favors more. Hence come the deep-seated uneasiness and vague agitation that can be observed in the South, and that contrast so sharply with the confidence and prosperity common to other parts of the Union. I am inclined to think that the hostile measures taken by the Southern provinces on a recent occasion are due to no other cause. Of all Americans, the inhabitants of the Southern States have the greatest interest in maintaining the Union; they would surely suffer most from being left to themselves; and yet they are the only citizens who threaten to break the bond of confederation. But it is easy to see that the South has given the Union four Presidents, Washington, Jefferson, Madison, and Monroe; that it perceives it is losing its federal influence; that the number of its representatives in Congress is shrinking from year to year, while those of the Northern and Western States are growing; and that the South, which is peopled with ardent and irascible men, is becoming more and more irritated and alarmed. Its citizens reflect on their present position and remember their past influence, with the melancholy uneasiness of men who suspect oppression. If they find a law of the Union that is not unequivocally favorable to their interests, they protest against it as an abuse of force; and if their ardent remonstrances go unheard, they threaten to leave an association that loads them with burdens while it deprives them of their due profits. “The tariff,” said the inhabitants of Carolina in 1832, “enriches the North, and ruins the South; for if this were not the case, to what can we attribute the continually increasing power and wealth of the North, with its inclement skies and arid soil; while the South, which may be styled the garden of America, is rapidly declining?” *q

problem: 'the latter' (the Federal Government) rendered as bare 'the government', which now reads as ambiguous and loses the explicit contrast with the bank.
replacement: The contest between the bank and its opponents is only an incident in the great struggle going on in America between the provinces and the central power, between the spirit of democratic independence and the spirit of gradation and subordination. I do not mean that the enemies of the bank are exactly the same individuals who attack the Federal Government on other points. But I assert that the attacks on the Bank of the United States spring from the same propensities that work against the Federal Government, and that the very numerous opponents of the bank are a deplorable symptom of the declining support for the Federal Government.
